title: Laravel: model attribute control, policy coverage, and deployed configuration

threat_model.actor: An authenticated user submitting fields the form never displayed and identifiers the interface never linked to, and an unauthenticated caller reaching whatever the deployment leaves readable
threat_model.asset: The columns a model write can set, the records a route binding resolves, the rows a scope was supposed to narrow, and the configuration an error page or a served file can disclose
threat_model.trust_boundary: The point where request data becomes model state, and the point where a route parameter becomes a loaded record — both of which the framework will perform for the developer without asking who the caller is
threat_model.failure_mode: A mass-assignment list is absent, emptied, or bypassed, or a record is resolved by identifier with no authorization check on the action that uses it, or a scope that supplies the ownership predicate is not applied on one path
threat_model.impact: A caller sets a column the interface never offered, reads or edits a record belonging to somebody else, or reads configuration and credentials from a page or file the deployment exposes

required_evidence: A Laravel application layout: an `artisan` entry point, a `composer.json` requiring the framework, and route definitions under `routes/`
At least one Eloquent model written from request data, or one route whose parameter resolves a record, or a configuration file read from environment values

versions: the attribute list can be declared as a `$fillable` or `$guarded` property, and current versions also accept a `Fillable` attribute on the class
`Model::preventSilentlyDiscardingAttributes` turns a discarded attribute into an exception, which is a development aid rather than a production control
signals: `$guarded` set to an empty array, which turns off the protection for that model entirely
A model with neither a fillable list nor a guarded list where the framework's default posture is the one the team assumed rather than the one it read
`create` or `update` called with the whole request bag rather than with validated data
`forceFill` or the force-create variants, which bypass the list by design
A global unguard call in a service provider, a seeder, or a console command that also runs in the request lifecycle
A validated payload whose rules cover the fields the form shows while the model accepts more
A controller action that loads and mutates a record with no gate call, no policy call, and no authorization middleware on its route
A form request whose authorize method returns true unconditionally, which is the scaffold default and is not by itself a check
Policy methods present for some abilities of a model and absent for others, so the uncovered ability is decided elsewhere or not at all
A gate callback registered to run before all others that returns true for a role, which short-circuits every policy for that role
Authorization applied on the controller while the same operation is also reachable from a queued job, a console command, or a second route
A resource route registered without the corresponding resource-authorization call, so only the actions someone remembered are covered

versions: child bindings can be scoped to their parent explicitly; without that, a nested parameter resolves globally rather than within the parent it appears under
signals: Implicit route-model binding resolving a record by identifier with no ownership predicate anywhere on the path
A nested route whose child parameter is not scoped to the parent, so an identifier from another owner still resolves
Route middleware applied to a group while a sibling route is registered outside it
A route registered in a file whose middleware group differs from the one the developer assumed
An identifier that is a sequential primary key exposed directly in the path, making enumeration trivial once the check is missing
A global scope supplying the ownership or tenancy predicate, together with calls that remove it
A local scope that must be remembered at each call site, where one query builder chain omits it
Raw query fragments carrying request-derived text: raw where, raw order, raw select, or a raw expression wrapper
A column name or sort direction taken from the request and placed into an order or where clause, which no binding can protect because it is structure rather than a value
A relationship traversed in a query or during serialisation that reaches rows the root query was never scoped to
Debug mode enabled in the deployed environment, which the configuration documentation states must be false in production because the error page discloses configuration values
A web server document root above the public directory, which places the environment file and application source inside the served tree
Storage or upload directories linked into the served tree without restricting what may execute from them
Unescaped output in a template rendering user-supplied content, where the escaping form was available and was not used
A model returned directly as an API response, so hidden-attribute configuration is the only thing standing between the database row and the client

boundary.subject: the authenticated user the request resolves, and the ownership relation between that user and the record
boundary.object: the attributes a write may set and the records a route parameter or a query may reach
boundary.invariant: Every attribute written is one the caller is permitted to set on that model, and every record reached through a route parameter or a query is one the caller is permitted to reach, established on the path that reaches it rather than on a sibling path

examples: Create or update called with the whole request bag
Global unguard active during a request
Implicit binding resolving by identifier with no ownership check
Nested child parameter resolved outside its parent
Query with the global scope removed
Builder chain that omits the ownership scope
Raw where or raw order carrying request text
Column name or sort direction taken from the request
Debug error page rendering configuration values
Environment file inside the served document root
Unescaped template output of user content
Model serialised directly into an API response

signals: For each write, ask which columns the caller can set and compare that with the columns the interface offers
For each record reached by identifier, ask what establishes that this caller may reach it, and on which line
Ask which paths reach the same operation — controller, job, command, second route — and whether each carries the same check
List every model with its attribute list and mark those with an empty guarded list, no list at all, or a force-write call anywhere
Find every create and update call and record whether its argument is validated data or the whole request bag
List every controller action and route and record the gate call, policy call, or authorization middleware that covers it, treating an unconditional authorize method as no check
Find every gate callback registered to run before the others and record which roles it short-circuits
List every route with a bound parameter and record whether an ownership predicate exists on that path, and for nested routes whether child scoping is enabled
Find every global scope and every call that removes one, and every raw query fragment carrying request-derived text
Read the deployed configuration for debug mode and for the document root, following environment resolution rather than reading defaults
State per model which attributes each role may set, and check the attribute list and the validation rules together express it
State per ability which principal may perform it against which record, and check both halves are enforced
Decide whether ownership is supplied by a scope, by a policy, or by an explicit predicate, and check the chosen mechanism is applied on every path
Establish which columns are security-relevant — role, owner, tenant, verification, balance — and whether any write path can reach them
Establish whether identifiers in routes are sequential, which decides how easily a missing check is exercised
Establish what the served document root contains and whether the environment file or application source is inside it
Against a local instance with two synthetic accounts, submit a write containing a security-relevant column and read the record back to see whether it was set
Request each bound route with the second account's identifier and record whether a record is returned
Exercise nested routes with a child identifier belonging to a different parent and record whether it resolves
Trigger an error and record whether the response contains configuration values

steps: Confirm explicit authorization and run a local instance with two synthetic accounts and synthetic records only
Record a baseline: perform each write and each read as the owning account and capture the request the interface produced
Replay each write with one added field naming a security-relevant column, against a record the test itself created, then read the record back and record whether the column changed
Replay each bound-route read and write with the second account's record identifier and record the status and body
Exercise nested routes with a child identifier that belongs to a different parent and record whether it resolves
Exercise every list and export path with filter, sort, and field parameters the interface does not offer, and record which are accepted
Trigger an error path and record exactly what the response contains, alongside the debug setting the instance ran with

Request the environment file and application source paths against the local document root only, to observe whether the served tree contains them, and never against an environment the authorization does not cover

false_positive_filters: The write is called with validated data whose rules enumerate exactly the permitted fields, so extra keys never reach the model regardless of the attribute list
The model declares a fillable list that excludes the security-relevant column, so an extra key is discarded rather than written — check the list before reporting the whole-bag call
The security-relevant column is set separately in code after the mass write, from server-derived state, so the caller's value would be overwritten even if it were accepted

The route carries authorization middleware, or the controller constructor applies the resource authorization for every action, so the absence of a call inside the method body is not the absence of a check
A gate or policy is invoked one call frame away, in a form request, a service, or an action class the controller delegates to; read the callee before concluding the check is missing
The ability has no gate or policy defined at all, in which case the framework's gate denies rather than allows, so an undiscovered policy fails closed and the real gap is an action that never asks
The bound model's query is narrowed by a global scope or by a relationship-based binding that already constrains it to the caller, so resolving by identifier cannot reach another owner's record
The nested route enables child scoping, so the child parameter is resolved within the parent rather than globally

The raw fragment contains only application-authored text, with every caller-derived value passed as a binding, and any caller-chosen column or direction mapped through an allowlist to a fixed identifier

Debug mode is false in the environment the deployment loads; a true value in a local environment file that production does not use is not a production finding, and the environment resolution has to be read to tell
The document root is the public directory, so the environment file and source sit above the served tree
The template escapes by default and the unescaped form is applied to content the application authored, not to user-supplied content

required_evidence: The write path end to end: the validation rules, the argument passed to the write, the model's attribute list, and any code that overwrites the column afterwards
The authorization surface for the action: the route middleware, the controller constructor, the method body, and any delegate that performs the check
A recorded request and the record read back afterwards, showing the attribute set or the record reached by a caller who should not be able to
For a scope claim, the executed query text showing the predicate absent, alongside the same path where it is present
The environment values actually loaded by the deployment, resolved through the environment chain rather than read from a default
refutation_tests: Read the validation rules and the model's attribute list together before reporting a whole-bag write, since either one alone can make the extra key harmless
Read the route definition, the controller constructor, and any delegate before reporting a missing authorization call, since the check frequently lives at one of those and not in the method body
Confirm whether an ability is defined at all, because an undefined ability is denied rather than allowed and the finding is then about the action that never asks
Check for a global scope or a relationship-constrained binding before asserting that resolving by identifier reaches another owner's record
Read the executed query rather than the builder chain before asserting a predicate is absent
Follow the environment resolution to the values the deployment loads before treating a local debug setting as a production one

root_causes: The framework will write whatever it is handed, so the attribute list is the only thing distinguishing an offered field from an accepted one, and it is easy to empty or bypass
Validation rules and the model attribute list are maintained separately, so one can be narrower than the other without anything failing
Route binding resolves a record before any authorization runs, which makes it feel as though the record was legitimately obtained
Nested routes read as scoped because of their path shape while the child parameter resolves globally unless scoping is enabled
Authorization is per action rather than per operation, so a second route, a job, or a command reaches the operation without it
Ownership is supplied by a scope that has an escape hatch, and the escape hatch is used where a wider result was momentarily convenient
Column names and sort directions are taken from the request because bindings appear to cover them, but structure cannot be bound
Debug mode and document root are deployment properties that the repository can suggest but not decide, so the reviewed value is not the one in force

variant_strategy.result_contract: EXACT | VARIANT | REFUTED | BLOCKED; exact and variant matches remain hypotheses until verified

remediation.canonical_invariant: Decide the writable attribute set and the reachable record set in the application, not in the request, and enforce both on the path that performs the operation rather than on a neighbouring one
patterns: Write models from validated data only, and keep the validation rules and the model attribute list aligned by a test rather than by convention
Declare an explicit fillable list on every model and treat an empty guarded list as a change that needs its own justification
Set ownership, role, tenant, and verification columns from server-derived state after the write, never from the request bag
Authorize in a place every route to the operation must pass — a policy invoked by the action class, or resource authorization applied in the controller constructor — rather than per method body
Enable child-binding scoping on nested routes so a child identifier is resolved within its parent
Constrain bound models with a scope or a relationship-based lookup so resolution by identifier cannot cross an ownership boundary
Keep ownership predicates in a query path with no escape hatch on request-serving code, and confine scope-removal to administrative paths that carry their own authorization
Map caller-chosen columns and sort directions through an allowlist to fixed identifiers, and bind every value
Serve from the public directory only, keep debug mode false in every reachable environment, and assert both in a deployment check rather than in a runbook
Return response resources rather than models, so a column added later does not appear in an API by default

assertions: The vulnerable object-update fixture declares a field list and then copies every key of the request body onto the persisted object anyway, so a privileged field arrives from the caller — the framework-neutral form of a write called with the whole request bag

The compensated object-update fixture keeps the identical whole-body copy and is safe only because the class declares `__slots__`, so undeclared attributes are rejected; the copy alone is not the finding and a reviewer who stops there reports a false positive

The vulnerable ownership fixture scopes the list path and re-fetches by primary key with no predicate on the export path, so one action enforces and its sibling does not — the framework-neutral form of a policy applied to one controller action and not the next
The remediated ownership fixture resolves objects through a call that requires the effective subject on both paths, and both paths still return the owner's data

The vulnerable ordering fixture parameterises values and still concatenates the caller's sort column and direction into the statement, which is what a request-supplied ordering term does regardless of the query builder in use
The remediated ordering fixture maps the column and direction through allowlists to fixed literals while keeping the legitimate sort options working

calibration.notes: This pack has not completed a reproducible benchmark run and makes no precision or recall claim.

limitations: The referenced fixtures are framework-neutral synthetic cases in plain Python; they exercise the invariants this pack anchors on and contain no PHP or Laravel code
Attribute-list defaults, authorization discovery, and binding-scoping behaviour have changed across major versions, so the project's version documentation is the authority rather than this pack
The document root, the environment values in force, and what the web server will execute are deployment properties the repository can suggest but not decide

First-party and community packages supply their own middleware, scopes, and policies that can either add or remove the constraints described here, and their configuration may live outside the reviewed code
A missing check found on one action does not establish the same gap on another; each path needs its own reachability evidence
